title: What Handy did: Memphis Blues and its publishers
summary: Carew's view that Handy showed money could be made from blues, and the story of Memphis Blues and Theron Bennett.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues

blocks.x: That was what started it. Well, Handy himself, I think that your friend, Abby Niles, helped along with that little thing. What Handy did, in there he admitted he heard, for instance, what he called the Atlanta blues, which was Make Me a Pallet on the Floor or something like that. He admitted that he heard a Negro thumping it out on a guitar at a railroad station once, and he took out his pad and he put down the tune. See, he admitted that. And also he was interviewed by Dorothy Scarborough, which was a book about American folk music. She went around and saw Mr. Handy and she asked him, she said, how did you get your blues, where did you get your blues? He said, I got my blues from songs I heard my Mammy sing. See, he says, I can tell you, and other places, of course, but he heard, he says, I can tell you where I got my idea of every one of my blues. So I said, the first one that said it, I said that what Handy did was to show that you can make money out of the blues. He published it, see. He published the Memphis blues and it got popular. But it didn't get popular very far. But he sold an edition, I guess, around Memphis and so forth. And then that publisher bought it from him. He assigned it to the other man, the publisher.

He couldn't get his hands on it. It hurt his feelings terribly that he had let that go and he couldn't get his hands on it again. But he did write the St. Louis blues after that. And that became still far more popular than Memphis. Yeah.
Well, Memphis is the one he lost.

Memphis is the one. Well, he got it back eventually. They didn't find it. He renewed it. He renewed it and got it. He renewed it and got it, yes. He came down here to the library and was so pleased when he made that renewal. It had a piece in the paper about it. It said his face shone and he was glad to get hold of that piece again. That's true. The other publisher there, Bennett was the name. Theron C. Bennett published that. I think he was out in Kansas City or someplace like that when he did it. But he went to Chicago, too, I think.
